title: US Internet Providers & Cell Phone Plans Compared
description: Compare US internet providers and cell phone carriers: Xfinity, Spectrum, AT&T, Verizon, T-Mobile, Starlink and prepaid brands, plus FCC labels and switching.
h1: US internet and cell phone plans compared
intro: In the US, home internet choice depends heavily on your address, with cable, fiber, fixed wireless and satellite competing street by street. Cell service is run by three national carriers and many prepaid brands.

image.alt: People crossing a street in Times Square, New York

blocks.title: Major US providers
blocks.intro: Cable and fiber providers are regional, so always check your address. Prepaid brands use one of the three national networks.

items.title: Xfinity
items.text: Comcast’s brand and one of the largest US home internet providers, mostly over cable.

items.title: Spectrum
items.text: Charter’s brand, selling cable internet across many states, with mobile on Verizon’s network.

items.title: AT&T
items.text: Runs a national mobile network plus AT&T Fiber and fixed wireless home internet in parts of the country.

items.title: Verizon
items.text: A national mobile carrier that also sells Fios fiber in the Northeast and 5G Home Internet.

items.title: T-Mobile
items.text: A national mobile carrier whose 5G Home Internet is a popular alternative to cable.
specs: 5G Home Internet, fiber in some areas

items.title: Starlink
items.text: SpaceX’s low-orbit satellite service, used where cable and fiber don’t reach.

items.title: Mint Mobile
items.text: Prepaid plans bought in multi-month blocks, running on T-Mobile’s network.

items.title: Visible
items.text: Verizon’s app-based, all-digital brand running on the Verizon network.

items.title: Cricket Wireless
items.text: AT&T’s prepaid brand, sold online and in stores.

items.title: Google Fi
items.text: Google’s phone service, running mainly on T-Mobile, popular with travelers for its international data.

items.title: Cox
items.text: A private cable provider serving parts of the South, Southwest and Midwest.

items.title: Metro by T-Mobile
items.text: T-Mobile’s prepaid brand with phone deals sold through stores.

sections.h2: Home internet types in the US
sections.html:
• Cable (Xfinity, Spectrum, Cox): widely available in cities and suburbs, with fast downloads.
  • Fiber (AT&T Fiber, Verizon Fios and others): the fastest option, with symmetrical speeds on many plans, where available.
  • 5G home internet (T-Mobile, Verizon, AT&T Internet Air): simple setup, no line needed; performance depends on local signal.
  • Satellite (Starlink and others): for rural areas where wired options don’t reach.

Check the FCC National Broadband Map to see which providers report service at your address.

Since 2024, internet providers must show a standard “broadband facts” label at the point of sale, listing the monthly price, introductory periods, one-time and monthly fees, and typical speeds and latency. It’s the easiest way to compare like with like. Read our guide.

Postpaid plans from AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile bundle perks and often device deals, billed after use. Prepaid brands (Cricket, Visible, Metro, Mint and others) are paid in advance and are often cheaper for the same network. Check whether a prepaid brand has lower data priority at busy times.

The federal Lifeline program offers a monthly discount on phone or internet service for eligible low-income households. The Affordable Connectivity Program stopped taking new funding in 2024. Some providers also run their own low-income plans. Check eligibility at the Lifeline Support site.

faqs.q: What counts as broadband in the US?
faqs.a: In 2024 the FCC raised its benchmark for fixed broadband to 100 Mbps download and 20 Mbps upload.

faqs.q: How do I keep my number when switching carrier?
faqs.a: Ask the new carrier to port your number. You’ll need your account number and a number transfer PIN from your current carrier. Don’t cancel the old line first.
